8.1 — Boss Design: Spec It First

Open the Project window, click into the search box and type boss. You will find nothing — no sprite, no prefab, no arena, no locked door. Every other unit this year handed you a starter asset and asked you to make it behave. This one hands you an empty search result. So today you do not open Unity at all: you write the document that decides what you will build for the next four lessons.

The Problem: The Boss Does Not Exist ~10 min

Most first bosses are designed backwards. A student opens Unity, drags a big sprite into the scene, scales it to 4×, adds a health number, and only then asks "what does it do?" The result is always the same: an enemy that is a wall with a number on it. It cannot be lost to, and it cannot be won against either — it is tedious in both directions.

The fix is not more discipline. It is ordering: decide the fight in words first, and let the code be the transcription of a decision you already made. Here is the honest inventory of what this project gives you to work with:

What already existsWhat you must create from nothing
Scenes: Start (index 0 — where the game begins; it holds the StatManager object, a Player, a Ground-tagged Quad and the tilemaps), Overworld (the hub, with the Canvas and your enemies), Platformer (your cave). All three are wired through SceneSwitch, and all three contain a Player. The arena — a room that does not exist yet. You will decide which scene hosts it and build it with the tilemap skills from 7.1.
Enemy art: Assets/Artwork/Character/Enemy/ holds OrcwithAxe1.png, OrcwithAxe2.png, a LoRTowerV2 tower sheet and Turret_Bullet.png. The Player folder holds Axe1, Axe2 and Shovel. The boss itself — no boss sprite exists. You will assemble one out of that art in 8.2, by scaling and recombining what is there. A scaled orc is a real answer; so is an oversized turret. A grey rectangle is also honest.
Systems you own: a StatManager singleton holding your player's health and coins (the refactor you did in 5.3), an ItemSpawner, a turret that fires projectiles, an enemy state machine, a lever with a UnityEvent. The lock, the win and the loss. There is no boss door in this project. There is a Switch.prefab carrying the working Lever.cs whose events are currently empty — you may reuse that machinery, but the door itself is yours to make in 8.5.
Read this before you spec a single number. The boss's health, your swing's damage and the player's max health are not independent. Your player's health is whichever number you chose in Unit 2 and then moved into StatManager in 5.3 — you own it, and it is not a value in this document. Your swing's damage is decided in 8.3. The only number you are choosing today is the boss's HP, and it only means something relative to the other two.

Socratic: What Makes a Boss a Boss?

  1. Name the last boss you actually lost to, then beat. What did it teach you before it attacked — and how did it teach you?
  2. A boss is a conversation: it asks a question with an attack, the player answers with a move, and the boss responds. What happens to that conversation if an attack has no answer the player can perform?
  3. You searched the Project for "boss" and found nothing. Where else in this project did an object you needed fail to exist — and what did you have to decide before you could build it?
  4. Your player's max health is whatever you chose, and the boss's damage is a decision you have not made yet. If the player may only make four mistakes in the whole fight, what does that fix about the boss's damage numbers?
  5. Which of these can you actually settle on paper: the boss's HP, your swing's damage, or how good the player is? Which one must you never balance against, and why?
  6. What kind of bug does a written spec prevent that a playtest cannot — the kind of flaw that no amount of tuning will repair?
Read Function-Level Examples ~15 min

A spec is a document that fixes an outcome and a budget, and leaves the machinery to whoever builds it. None of these examples is from a video game. Read each one for the shape of the thinking, then ask what the equivalent sentence is for your boss.

Example 1 — A siege engine's spec sheet (the numbers are the design):

// A trebuchet is specified as: 90 m range, 8-second reload,
// 300 kg counterweight. The crew drills to those numbers.
// Nobody specifies the wood.

Example 2 — A bottling line's throughput (one number constrains every station):

// The line is specified as 40,000 bottles per hour.
// Every station's cycle time must fit inside that.
// One station out of budget makes the whole line's number a lie.

Example 3 — A stadium scoreboard cue sheet (cause left, effect right):

// "Q4 00:00 - sound horn, show FINAL" is a cue.
// The operator is told the cue, never the wiring.

Example 4 — A stage manager's lighting cue (one name, many machines):

// "LX 12 - preshow blackout" touches forty dimmer racks.
// The cue has a name so the caller never has to know which ones.

Example 5 — A recipe card is a spec (outcome and budget, not method):

// "Serves 4. 20 minutes." That is the whole contract.
// The pan, the flame and the order of operations are the cook's problem.

Predict Before You Write the Spec

  1. Which of the five examples above specifies a cycle time — a delay between repetitions? Which part of your fight is that same idea?
  2. The cue sheet names effects and never the wiring. What is the equivalent of "the wiring" in your boss, and why should the person playing your game never need to know it?
  3. The bottling line's single number constrains every station. Which single number in your boss fight must every attack's timing fit inside?
  4. The recipe card fixes the outcome and the budget but not the method. Which of the six parts of your boss spec is explicitly a method decision that you are allowed to change later without breaking the others?
  5. Every one of these documents was written before the machine was built. What is the cost of discovering a bad fight-length number after the boss is coded instead of before?
Read the Docs: The Six-Part Spec ~20 min

Here are the six parts, what each one is for, and the failure each one prevents. Write all six today, on paper, before you touch Unity.

PartWhat it fixesThe failure it prevents
1. Identity One sentence naming what the thing is and how it behaves: "The Cave Warden: slow, huge, guards the exit, telegraphs everything." A boss with no personality becomes a stat block, and a stat block is never scary.
2. Health economy Boss HP, against your swing's damage from 8.3, against the seconds between openings. Hits needed × seconds between openings = fight length. A fight that is over in twelve seconds, or one that outlasts the player's patience.
3. Phases (two or three) What changes at each threshold — a new attack, a faster rhythm, a hazard waking up. A fight whose second half is identical to its first, which players read as "the boss has more HP than personality."
4. Attacks Two or three per phase, each with four named properties: telegraph (what tells you it is coming), timing (how long you have to react), counterplay (the move that beats it), punishment (what a mistake costs). The "dodge randomly or take the hit" attack — decoration that reads as unfairness.
5. Tells and fairness The rule from 7.5: a boss is a level that fights back, so it must be readable. Same signposting standard you applied to the cave. A fight you can only win by memorising it, which is not the same thing as being hard.
6. Arena Where the fight happens, how the player enters, whether they may leave, and which hazards the boss ignores but the player must respect. An arena that is a featureless box, or a fight the player simply walks away from.
Architectural specification: the fight's arithmetic.
  • Write the target fight length first, in seconds, and defend the number. A fight that is too short cannot teach its own patterns; a fight that is too long has to invent difficulty out of repetition.
  • How many seconds out of every ten is your player actually allowed to attack? That is the inverse of your boss's attack pressure. Estimate it from the rhythm you are planning, then write it down — you will check it against the real build in 8.4.
  • With that fraction fixed, how many hits must land for the fight to reach its target length? That number, times your swing's damage from 8.3, is the boss's HP.
  • Why is the boss's HP the last number you write rather than the first, even though it is the one the player stares at?
  • Where does the player's own health come from in this calculation — a value you invent today, or the max health already sitting in your StatManager? What does that tell you about how many mistakes the fight should allow?
Architectural specification: the arena.
  • Which scene hosts the fight? Start holds the StatManager — the object that keeps your health and coins alive across scenes — while Overworld already has hazards and the Canvas, and Platformer is your cave. Which of those facts matters most for an arena, and what does choosing each scene cost you?
  • Where does the player enter, and can they leave the same way? If your arena has two open exits, what is stopping the player from simply walking out mid-fight?
  • There is no boss door in this project. You will build one in 8.5. Decide now whether the fight is locked (a barrier appears), gated (the way onward opens only when the boss dies) or open (the player may always flee). Write one sentence defending your choice.
  • Which hazards does the boss ignore but the player must respect? Why does a hazard that hurts both of you usually read as a bug rather than a feature?
  • The room's size is a difficulty knob nobody remembers to turn. Sketch it in tiles using the numbers you already know: your player's walk speed and your jump's apex height from 6.3. How wide must the room be before your boss's fastest attack is dodgeable by running rather than by luck?
Architectural specification: the attack list.
  • For each attack, write the telegraph as something the player can see: a colour flash, a wind-up pose, a sound. "It just happens" is not a telegraph.
  • For each attack, write the counterplay as a sentence naming the player's move and the number that makes it possible: "jump the wave; the wave is one tile tall and the jump apex is two."
  • Is the counterplay available in every phase, or does a later phase remove it? Removing an answer is a legitimate escalation — removing all of them is not.
  • Count your states: a boss with six states is a large build. How many did you write, and which one will you cut first if the build is not working by the end of 8.2?
  • Which single attack is your boss's signature — the one a player would describe if asked what the fight was about? If you cannot name one, you have written a list rather than a boss.
Bug Hunt: Spec Review ~15 min

Bug Hunt: Finding the Holes in a Fight That Does Not Exist Yet

  1. Hand your spec to a partner and have them play the boss in their head, attack by attack. Ask them to say the counterplay out loud for each one. Which attack could they not answer — and what does that silence tell you?
  2. Do the arithmetic out loud: if the player may attack one second in every five, and the boss needs twenty hits, how long is the fight? Is that inside or outside the target you wrote in part 2?
  3. Phase three of your spec adds a faster rhythm and a new attack at the same time. How many new things is the player expected to learn at once, and what does 7.5 say about introducing more than one new idea per beat?
  4. Read your telegraphs again and find any that are only visible in the Console. Which of your tells would a player who is not reading the Console completely miss?
  5. Your arena spec says the player enters here and the fight happens there. Measure the room on your sketch against your player's walk speed: how many seconds does it take to cross? Is there anywhere in the room that is genuinely safe?
  6. Find the sentence in your spec that would be hardest to change later — the one a different decision would invalidate. Is that a load-bearing decision or an accident of ordering?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Commit the Design

  1. Type the final spec as BOSS_SPEC.md in your repo, next to the code it will govern. Why does a design document belong in version control rather than in a notebook you will lose?
  2. Sketch the arena on paper. Mark where the player enters, where the boss waits, and where — if anywhere — the way onward opens. Which tilemap from 7.1 will you build it on?
  3. Which single thing will you cut first if the build runs long, and why does naming that sacrifice in advance make a design document earn its keep?
  4. Commit and push with a message naming the lesson: "8.1: boss spec + arena sketch". Why is the commit message part of the deliverable?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain why the boss, the arena and the door must be built rather than found — and name what this project actually ships you
  • Write all six parts of a boss spec: identity, economy, phases, attacks, tells, arena
  • Derive the boss's HP from your swing's damage and your target fight length instead of guessing it
  • Say the counterplay sentence out loud for every attack you wrote
  • Name the scene that will host the fight, and justify it against what each of the three scenes already contains
  • Commit and push your BOSS_SPEC.md
